doc.title: Earl May interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2001

chapter: Gloria Lynne, Milt Hinton and later work
title: Effect of pop and rock; encouraging young players
summary: Pop has not affected May much; he finds many young players sound alike and plans to mix them with seasoned players.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Right. How has the changes in pop and rock music affected what you’ve done over the years? Or has it?

I don’t think it’s really affected me very much. But I mean I will have to say that I have a lot of respect for young people. There are some that come out of school and they really have a lot to say. And then there are others that come out of school, the majority, where it’s sad to say but they all seem to sound alike. I can’t distinguish — the piano players all sound the same, the bass players all sound the same, and it’s sad in that way. But there are some that come out like I’m trying to start — help them by having one other professional, when I say professional, one other seasoned player in a group where we’d feature a saxophone player or a singer and when the rest of them will be young people. When we’re doing like things in jazz clubs and things like that. So we’re going to start that kind of thing. Because just to boost people. If I knew that you had a son that’s twelve years old or something like that and was trying to play harmonica, I would ask you to please bring him in and come and sit in with us. Just trying to encourage the young people to play and be a part of jazz.
